summary:
LunaOS is an interactive lunar habitat simulation where you take command of a Moon outpost and make the engineering decisions needed to keep its crew alive for 30 simulated days.

✨ Features

Mission Control: Monitor crew status, resource reserves, habitat conditions, and mission progress.
Resource Management: Balance oxygen, water, food, and battery energy.
Systems & Engineering: Configure life-support recycling, greenhouse production, scientific activity, and maintenance.
Upgrades & Repairs: Invest mission credits in improving habitat systems and resolving faults.
Dynamic Events: Respond to unexpected events that introduce new challenges and decisions.
Mission Log: Track events, decisions, warnings, and daily developments.
Mission Analysis: Review mission performance, resource trends, system issues, and important decisions.
Interactive Forecasts: Explore projected energy reserves and resource trends.

🛰️ How to Play

Initialize your mission: Choose your crew size and difficulty level.
Monitor your habitat: Check available resources, system conditions, and warnings.
Configure your systems: Adjust recycling, agriculture, research, and maintenance settings.
Make decisions: Respond to mission events, purchase upgrades, and repair faults.
Advance each day: Observe how your decisions affect the habitat.
Complete the mission: Survive all 30 simulated days and review your mission debrief.
details:
Project Details

LunaOS is an interactive lunar habitat simulation designed to help students understand the engineering trade-offs involved in sustaining a crewed outpost on the Moon. The player takes the role of a mission commander and manages a 30-day lunar mission, balancing oxygen, water, food, energy, radiation protection, maintenance, and scientific activity.

The simulation is built around cause and effect. Each day, the player decides how to configure the habitat, allocate resources, respond to unexpected events, and invest in upgrades. These decisions affect the habitat over time, so maximizing one system can create pressure elsewhere. For example, increasing agricultural production can improve future food availability while also increasing energy and water demands. The mission can ultimately succeed or fail depending on how effectively the player manages these interconnected systems.

The main benefit of LunaOS is that it turns abstract space-engineering concepts into something students can experiment with directly. Instead of only reading about the challenges of lunar habitation, players can make decisions, see their consequences, and review their performance through resource graphs, mission logs, and a post-mission analysis.

The intended impact is to make STEM concepts surrounding human space exploration more approachable and engaging for younger learners. LunaOS focuses particularly on systems thinking: showing that a lunar mission is not a collection of independent problems, but a network of systems where every decision has consequences.

I developed LunaOS using Python, Streamlit, Pandas, and Plotly, with Git and GitHub for version control and deployment. Python handles the simulation engine and resource calculations, while Streamlit provides the interactive interface. Pandas is used for organizing mission history and Plotly is used for visualizing resource and energy trends. The project is deployed as a web application so it can be accessed without specialized hardware.

The creative aspect of LunaOS is its combination of a game-like decision loop with an operating-system-inspired interface. Rather than presenting the player with a conventional dashboard, LunaOS is designed as a fictional lunar habitat operating system, with mission control, system management, events, and post-mission analysis forming one continuous experience. I also designed the simulation so that the player is encouraged to understand why a decision worked or failed rather than simply receiving a score.

While developing the project, I considered scientific accuracy, accessibility, simplicity for younger learners, meaningful resource trade-offs, usability, and the limitations of a simplified simulation. Real lunar engineering is far more complex than the model presented in LunaOS, so I distinguish research-based concepts from simplified game assumptions. The goal is not to reproduce a real NASA mission, but to create an educational environment where students can explore the kinds of interconnected decisions that real missions require.
